source.title: SAE Training Dataset Influence in Feature Matching and a Hypothesis on Position Features

record.tranche_reason: The study compares decoder-weight feature matches across SAE dictionary sizes, a different measurement from directly tracking whether a coarse feature splits into children and partitions its inputs.
record.gate_note: The study reports decoder-based feature matching ratios and derived feature-count differences for different dictionary sizes. It does not measure which inputs each feature activates on, or whether several larger-dictionary features jointly partition a smaller feature’s inputs. Position-activation analyses, and comparisons of datasets, seeds, architectures, and sparsity, do not bear directly on the size-splitting versions and are not rows.
record.test_reason: Compares decoder-direction matches between Top-k SAEs of 3,072, 6,144 and 12,288 latents on GPT2-small layer 8. This is a geometric, not activation-based, check of how latents relate across dictionary sizes. It bears weakly on V5 (larger SAEs contain many latents with no close smaller-SAE counterpart) and only indirectly on V1.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but incomplete. The main conclusion is that the training dataset affects the learned feature set more than seed, sparsity or architecture. On size, the author finds that smaller-dictionary features are mostly contained in larger ones. Contrary to their hypothesis, cross-seed matching drops at larger sizes, which they attribute to size-dependent abstraction (feature splitting) rather than convergence to an ideal feature set. Splitting itself is not demonstrated.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses thresholded cosine similarity between decoder weights to compare features across SAE settings; it does not directly track feature inputs across a dictionary-size intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: Dictionary size and training dataset affect matching ratios; the authors also report effects from seed, sparsity, and SAE architecture, but these other comparisons are not rows for the size-splitting versions.

fits_no_version.finding: Cross-seed matching ratio falls as dictionary size grows: 83.46%/71.37% at 3,072 versus 54.85%/55.65% at 12,288 (OWT/TinyStories). The author attributes this to size-dependent abstraction levels and feature splitting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Seed-to-seed consistency of SAE latents decreases with dictionary size, so larger dictionaries do not converge to a fixed feature set.

record.problems: Only GPT2-small is studied. Feature matching uses a thresholded cosine measure and does not test input-set coverage. The authors note that not using the Hungarian algorithm may overestimate similarity and make the numbers not strictly comparable with prior studies. Table values are flattened in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: Activation-position analyses, dataset-only comparisons, seed-only comparisons, architecture comparisons, and sparsity comparisons were left out because they do not measure dictionary-size splitting or the V5 combination claim. No Table 1 or Table 2 size-comparison results were omitted.

untested.parts: Whether a coarse latent is replaced by several finer latents that cover its inputs. Only top-1 cosine to the other dictionary is measured; no activations and no one-to-many mapping.
All of it: only GPT2-small with self-trained SAEs.
All of it: no hierarchy or family analysis.
All of it: no parent/child firing analysis.
Whether larger latents decompose into combinations of smaller latents, and whether unmatched latents are novel rather than split children.
All of it. Matryoshka SAEs are only suggested as future work.

missing.what: Seed-comparison matching ratios by dictionary size (Table 1 seed rows), which the author ties to feature splitting and non-convergence of feature sets
missing.locator: Section 4.2.2, Table 1 seed rows and following paragraph

record.verdict_notes: An informal LessWrong post (score 4) by a single author. Matching uses no Hungarian algorithm, which the author says may overestimate similarity. There is no baseline (e.g., random-direction match rates), so the 0.7 threshold's chance level is unknown. The V1 rows are set to cannot_determine because the cosine-match measure cannot distinguish a persisting parent from near-direction children.

versions.untested_parts: The study compares feature directions across dictionary sizes, but does not identify parent-to-child splits or test whether the larger features collectively cover or partition the smaller feature’s inputs.
No large models or open SAE releases are tested for the size-splitting pattern.
No nested feature families or hierarchy of concepts are tested.
No parent-child activation overlap or absorption behavior is tested.

Cross-size feature matching bears on feature consistency, but the study does not test whether larger latents decompose into combinations of smaller latents, nor establish that unmatched latents are novel.
The study does not test whether splitting is an artifact of the SAE objective or compare Matryoshka SAEs.

rows.operation_detail: Compared decoder-weight feature matches across dictionary sizes
rows.note: The table labels the comparison “12,288 in 3,072”; the text says smaller-dictionary features were often contained in larger dictionaries. This ratio does not measure input coverage or a split.
rows.check: Only 25.56% of 12,288 latents have a ≥0.7 cosine match among 3,072 latents, consistent with larger SAEs adding latents. A top-1 cosine cannot separate split children from novel latents, and V1's split structure is not measured. Drop V1.

relation.reason: Reports matching ratios across dictionary sizes and links them to splitting.

tranche.reason: The study uses one step of the V5 original's method (max decoder cosine at 0.7 on GPT-2), but it runs no stitching/MSE or meta-SAE test. The comparison sits inside a study of training-setting influence, with its own Top-k SAEs and datasets. That fits T2 (different method, related question), not T1.

source_check.notes: The 'X in Y' direction is confirmed by Table 2 (12288x25.56% - 3072x89.22% = 400): it gives the share of X's latents matched in Y. The author says skipping Hungarian matching may overestimate similarity. Cross-seed matching (Table 1) falls with size, from 83.46%/71.37% at 3072 to 54.85%/55.65% at 12288. This bears on V5 but has no rows. The TinyStories value 71.37% appears for both 6144 and 3072, possibly a source typo.

statements.problem: 'May be split children' is the catalog's hedged reading, not the author's. The author ties feature splitting to the cross-seed drop, not to the dictionary-difference ratios. Acceptable as worded.
